entries.title: Room for their own movement
entries.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
entries.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

entries.title: A conversation with your baby
entries.summary: Answer a sound, smile or gesture, then pause. Your baby’s next response can guide the conversation.

Raspberries, bubbles and changes in volume are part of the vocal play the authors describe. There is no need to ask for a particular sound or word.

entries.title: When they pull away from care
entries.summary: If your baby resists dressing or a change, notice what they may be asking for. When care cannot wait, explain and proceed as gently as possible.
entries.cue: Your baby twists away, protests or wants to keep playing.
detail: The authors consider timing, a wish to participate, or a feeling about being handled. If there is time, a pause to finish play, a small choice, or a song shared for connection may help.
A guess can stay a guess: “You’re pulling away. Would you like a moment?” The baby need not agree for their feeling to matter.

detail: Holding the baby, meeting their gaze and noticing their response are forms of connection in the book’s account. This possibility belongs to different primary caregivers and feeding arrangements.

The authors acknowledge that some people choose not to breastfeed, that difficulties may call for specialist support, and that feeding not going as hoped can bring grief. The relationship is not limited to one way of offering milk.

entries.title: A familiar shape to the day
entries.summary: The authors look for a baby’s changing rhythm of feeding, play and sleep, with familiar cues for transitions. Their pattern is a guide to noticing, not a timetable.
entries.cue: You are trying to understand what your baby needs next.
detail: Their usual wake–feed–play–sleep sequence varies as the baby grows. Sometimes play comes before a feed, and travel or changes at home can shift what is familiar.
A repeated phrase or song can signal what is coming. The authors suggest coordinating with other caregivers where possible, while keeping the baby’s own cues in view.

Family rituals can be part of that familiar world too: a regular park visit, a special breakfast or a celebration from one or more family cultures. The baby can be included before they can contribute much themselves.

entries.summary: The authors begin with this baby’s tired signs and the help they need, in a safe, comfortable sleep setting. A short familiar routine can offer connection; falling asleep is not a performance.

They describe gradually changing help when both baby and adult are ready, and explicitly say it is okay if feeding or rocking is currently part of settling. Their broader discussion also acknowledges night waking during the first year.
The book’s sleep-surface recommendations contain tensions with its own safety box; this account concerns responsive support and does not choose a sleeping arrangement.

entries.title: Let goodbye be something they can recognize

A familiar book or brief shared ritual can become part of goodbye. When there is time, the book makes room for an unhurried hug. When there is not, it describes acknowledging sadness and gently handing care over.
